'''Rolf Noskwith''' (19 June 1919 – 3 January 2017) was a British businessman who during the [[Second World War]] worked under [[Alan Turing]] as a [[cryptographer]] at the [[Bletchley Park]] British military base.<ref name="Sugarman 2012">
{{cite web
 |url         = https://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jsource/ww2/bletchleyjews.html
 |title       = Jewish Personnel at Bletchley Park in World War Two
 |last1       = Sugarman
 |first1      = Martin
 |year        = 2012
 |work        = Jewish Virtual Library
 |publisher   = The American-Israeli Cooperative Enterprise
 |location    = Chevy Chase, Maryland, USA
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20120713104011/http://www.jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jsource/ww2/bletchleyjews.html

 |access-date  = 8 August 2012
 |url-status     = dead
 |df          = dmy-all

==Early life and education==
Noskwith's parents, Chaim (Charles) and Malka (née Ginsberg), were Eastern European-born Jews who set up a clothing manufacturing company in Germany. Seeing that the political and economic conditions were worsening, they sold their business and emigrated to England in 1932, along with their children.<ref name="Sugarman 2012" /> The family created another textile company, [[Charnos]], in [[Ilkeston]], [[Derbyshire]], England,<ref>{{cite web| url=http://www.businessmagnet.co.uk/company/charnosplc-6226.htm | title=Charnos P.L.C. | website=Businessmagnet.co.uk | location=UK | access-date=7 January 2017 }}</ref> that would become the basis of Noskwith's post-war life. Noskwith was educated at [[Nottingham High School]] and [[Trinity College, Cambridge]].{{citation needed|date=April 2020}}

==Service in Second World War==
Initially, he was not accepted for military service, but after his third attempt, he was accepted to work as a translator and cryptographer at the Bletchley Park facility.<ref name="Sugarman 2012" /> His first attempt to work as a codebreaker was turned down because of his German birth and upbringing, but it seems that the security eligibility rules were revised in May 1941 thereby enabling him to enlist.{{sfn|Seberg-Montefoire (2000)|p=152}}

===Government Code and Cypher School, Bletchley Park===
After being interviewed by [[C. P. Snow]] and [[Conel Hugh O'Donel Alexander|Hugh Alexander]], Noskwith was recruited to [[Bletchley Park]] and arrived in June 1941.{{sfn|Noskwith (2011)|p=185}} He worked in [[Hut 8]], focusing on the German navy's [[Enigma machine]], decrypting the [[Kriegsmarine]]'s coded wireless traffic from 1941 to 1945,{{sfn|Seberg-Montefoire (2000)|pp=152–153}} and subsequently on other ciphers. He joined the [[Crib (cryptanalysis)|crib]] subsection, headed by [[Shaun Wylie]].{{sfn|Noskwith (2011)|p=185}} One of Noskwith's noted talents was lining up cribs with cipher text strips, to see if they matched.{{sfn|Seberg-Montefoire (2000)|p=152}}

Noskwith's biggest accomplishment was breaking the Naval Enigma [[Officer (armed forces)|Offizier]] settings. He created a [[Known-plaintext attack|crib]] based on the letters 'EEESSSPATRONE' and had placed into queue to be crunched by Bletchley's [[bombe]] analogue computers. The letter pairings referred to colour-coding used by German ships' flares as "[[Identification friend or foe|friend or foe]]" detection. When the crib worked, it allowed the [[Allies of World War II|Allied forces]] to read German messages sent to and from [[Kriegsmarine]] officers.{{sfn|Seberg-Montefoire (2000)|p=153}}

Noskwith recalled that most people were addressed by their first name there:{{sfn|Hinsley & Stripp (1993)|p=119}} the two exceptions were Alan Turing, known as "Prof"; and F.A. Kendrick, whom he was surprised to see listed in the index of Hinsley and Stripp's book ''Codebreakers'' as Kendrick, Tony.{{sfn|Hinsley & Stripp (1993)|p=317}}

==Later life and death==
Beginning in 1946, Noskwith worked for [[Charnos]], the textile company founded by his father, and became its chairman in 1952.<ref name="Sugarman 2012" /> Around the year 2000, he was made non-executive chairman of Charnos plc.{{citation needed|date=January 2017}}

Noskwith died on 3 January 2017, aged 97.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://jewishnews.timesofisrael.com/rolf-noskwith-rip/|title=Jewish Bletchley Park code-breaker dies aged 97|date=3 January 2017| newspaper=[[Jewish News]] |access-date=2017-01-03}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://israelnewsonline.org/jewish-bletchley-park-code-breaker-rolf-noskwith-dies-aged-97/|title=Jewish Bletchley Park code-breaker Rolf Noskwith dies aged 97|date=4 January 2017|website=Israel News Online|access-date=2017-01-04}}</ref><ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/obituaries/2017/01/06/rolf-noskwith-bletchley-park-codebreaker-obituary/ | title=Rolf Noskwith, Bletchley Park codebreaker – obituary | newspaper=[[Daily Telegraph]] | location=UK | date=6 January 2017 }}</ref> He is thought to have been the last surviving cryptographer of Bletchley Park at the time of his death.{{citation needed|date=January 2017}} Shortly after his death, ''[[The Jewish Chronicle]]'' published a tribute to Noskwith and other Jewish codebreakers by the director of [[Government Communications Headquarters|GCHQ]] [[Robert Hannigan]], who described their contribution as "out of all proportion to the size of the Jewish community in Britain at the time". Noting the contribution of Jewish staff at Bletchley to the foundation of Israel after World War II he referred to Noskwith's offer of his services in 1947 to [[Walter Eytan]], who responded "of codebreakers we have plenty!".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thejc.com/life/the-secret-story-of-the-jewish-codebreakers-who-helped-win-the-war-gomeqgxc|title=The Secret Story of the Jewish codebreakers who helped win the war|last=Hannigan|first=Robert|date=2017-02-26| work=[[The Jewish Chronicle]] |access-date=2017-05-09}}</ref>

Following Noskwith's death, a two-page mathematical manuscript handwritten by [[Alan Turing]] was found among his papers and sold at [[Bonhams]] auction house in London for £44,000 to [[King's College, Cambridge]], Turing's former college.<ref>{{cite journal| first1=Jonathan P. | last1=Bowen | author-link1=Jonathan Bowen | first2=B. Jack | last2=Copeland | author-link2=Jack Copeland | title=A newly discovered mathematical manuscript by Alan Turing | journal=[[FACS FACTS]] | volume=2023-2 | pages=6–9 | date=July 2023 | url=https://www.bcs.org/media/10894/facs-jul23.pdf | publisher=[[British Computer Society|BCS]] }}</ref>
